about: The words of the chain saga_neustria_west, the saint who left his island (cards: Data/encounters/chain_saga_neustria_west_793.json; page: Design/content/chains/saga_neustria_west.md). Written 6 Oct 2026: a draft for the user to overwrite. Nothing is quoted from a modern translation: what Ermentarius, the charters and the annals say is given in our own words from Design/content/dossiers/herio.md. Every card has an art.<card id> entry for the artist, and every ending an art.chain_saga_neustria_west.ending.<name>.

entries.text: The abbot's wall
A bank of earth and oak stakes is going up round Saint Philibert's monastery, and the lead is coming off the church roof. The salt is the same price as ever.
Half the stalls in the choir are empty. From early spring to the end of autumn most of the brothers are at Deas on the mainland, and the island keeps a few for the lamps and the salt.
One of the abbey's six river boats lies at the quay loading oak stakes, toll-free and in a hurry. The salt brother from Herio is seeing them counted aboard.
The abbot is building a wall round a house he takes us out of every spring. I have set riddles all my life and I cannot answer that one.
The lead is off the north aisle and lying in a shed at Furca, over the water. A roof is the last thing a house sells and the first thing it hides.
Four loads of oak, squared, before the saint's feast. I pay in salt or in silver. I do not pay for bark.
He wants four loads more, squared, before the saint's feast. He pays in salt or silver. He has told me twice that he does not pay for bark.
And the Bordeaux oil man has not sent his ship this year. He is owed for nine jars, and he has heard what swims in our bay in fine weather.
Take the abbot's order: four loads of squared oak for the wall
Lend your crew to the bank for a day, for bread and the salt brother's talk
Load your salt and ask nothing
The order is cut on a tally: four loads of squared oak, to be landed here. The abbot measures your hold with his rod before he lets you go, out of habit.

Your men carry turf until dusk and eat the abbey's bread. Natalis talks the whole day. He says the wall is so the saint has somewhere to be left from, and gives you a riddle about the wind to take the taste away.
You load salt. Behind you a mallet goes on driving stakes, one every few breaths, until you are out of hearing.
Nine jars owed
Leontius the oil seller, Felix's son, has lamp oil in his store that should have gone north to the salt island. He is not sending his ship.
You have been to the island. Then you have seen my oil burning. Three lamps, day and night, and nine jars of it not paid for.
My steersman saw long ships among the islands at the turn of spring. He is a brave man. He came straight home to tell me so.
My father sold to that house for thirty years and was paid in salt every time. I would like to be the son who was paid, and not the son who put a lamp out.
The jars stand in straw under the city wall, each as high as a child, stopped with clay and scratched with a cross for the saint.
Carry four jars north on his trust, the freight paid now
Buy six jars for yourself at his price
Carry only his letter of demand to the abbot
Four jars go aboard wedged in straw, the abbey's and not yours. Leontius pays the freight in pennies and cuts a tally for the cellarer: thirteen jars owed now, payable in salt.
Six jars, yours, at a price he would not give a stranger. He says to stand them upright, and that he does not ask where oil goes.
The letter is short. Leontius reads it to you so that you know what you carry: nine jars, thirty years, and the name of his father. He pays you six pennies to put it in the abbot's own hand.
The saint's feast
On the feast of Saint Philibert nine ships of the Northmen came to the island, and the island fought them from the ninth hour until evening.
The vigil was kept all night. At the ninth hour a boy on the east head shouts, and there they are: nine sails, low, coming round the point on a flat sea.
They will beach on the ebb and think the sand is theirs. Horse on the hard ground, foot at the gate. Shipman, stand or go, but do it now.
The rakers' children are in the dunes with nothing between them and that beach. Your boat floats. Ours are on the sand.
Trampled sand, the bones of horses, a long new mound above the tide line. The fight is over, and is already told three ways.
One of ours is dead. The brothers say four hundred and eighty-four of theirs. I buried what there was to bury, and I did not reach that number.
The monks say the saint went out by the west gate in white, with a golden sword. I was at the west gate. I saw the count's horses. They were enough.
A flat sea brought nine. The next flat sea can bring ninety, and the ebb will keep the count on the far shore while they dig.
In the basilica three lamps burn at the head of the marble coffin. The oil is Leontius's. The cellarer tells you so twice.
Stand at the west gate with the abbey's men
Take the rakers' children across the lagoon in your boat
Keep off until it is over, then help bury what the tide left

They come up the sand at the ninth hour and are still coming at dusk, fewer each time. The count's horses break them on the hard ground. Afterwards he gives each man who held the gate a handful of pennies, and looks at your face long enough to know it again.
You hold the gate. A spear butt breaks two of your ribs somewhere between the ninth hour and evening, and you see the end of it sitting down. The count sends his own man to bind you.
Three trips over the lagoon with the boat full of children and one old woman who will not let go of her rake. You hear the fight and see none of it. Martinus counts them off the far bank by name.
You dig with the abbey's men above the tide line. There are a good many dead and nothing like the number the brothers give. Nobody who is digging argues with it.
The ebbs
Abbot Hilbod is at the bishop's house in Namnetis, back from King Pippin's assembly with leave to take Saint Philibert off the island.
You sail that bay. Tell me before the abbot does: can a horseman get over to the island when he is needed, or only when the sea allows?
The king's great men said it plainly. Because of the ebbs our men cannot always reach the island. The Northmen can, whenever the sea is calm. So the saint goes where men can reach him.
After Pentecost, on a morning flood, before the summer calms. To Furca by ship, in the coffin, marble and all. Then on men's shoulders to Deas.
I held that sand once, with horses that swam half the way. I will not promise it twice. Show me a road over the water and I will put men on his wall.
The count knows your face from the west gate, and says so to the bishop.
And the people of the island? They are not the abbey's people. Has anyone told them?
I will not be the abbot under whom the founder was dug up and thrown in the sea. I would sooner be the abbot who left.
Offer your ship for the crossing
Say the channel can be marked and a ferry kept at Furca, and offer to prove it
Say nothing in this hall. Go and tell the island

Hilbod asks what your ship carries at the most, and what a marble coffin with a man in it weighs. He answers the second himself. He counts out half a pound of pennies for a frame, rollers and pitch, and names the tide.

The count laughs, then stops. He will come to the far shore before Pentecost with twelve horsemen and watch. The withies, the flat boat and the men to pole it are yours to find. The abbot says only that he has his leave already.
You tell the bishop the ebbs are as the abbot says, which is true. Gunhard watches you go with the look of a man who has had half an answer.
A road over the water

The monastery's channel dries at the ebb and fills on the flood. Between the two there is an hour when a flat boat on a marked line could bring horsemen across. The count has come to the far shore to see it done.
Old Ursus taught me the channel with a pole and a clout on the ear. A withy every forty paces, and the bend marked double. They will stand until the first big tide of spring.
If the count's men can cross, the monks may stay. If the monks stay, somebody buys our salt who also says Mass. I will cut your withies.
Twelve horses and their riders, across and back, on the tide you name. Drown one and I go home.
I have the king's leave. I will watch. I measured that channel myself, shipman, and I did not like the number.
Set the marks and bring the horsemen over on the half tide
Pay Martinus and four rakers to sound every yard first, then try it
It cannot be proved in one spring. Tell Hilbod he was right

Four horses to a crossing, three crossings, and back again before the channel is knee deep. The count rides off the boat last and says nothing until he is on dry sand. Then he says twenty men, changed at each new moon, and has his steward pay you for the ferrying.

The second boatload takes the bend wide. A grey horse goes over the side in the one deep place and is not seen again; its rider is pulled out by the hair. The count goes home. You pay half the horse. Hilbod asks, not unkindly, whether he may have your ship now.
Hilbod nods. He says a man who measures a thing and then says the number is rarer than a miracle, and that he still needs a ship for the tenth day after Pentecost.
What the island is left with
On the salt heaps the rakers ask you what the monks will not tell them: is the saint going, and is the wall to be manned after.
You were at Namnetis. Is he going? Do not tell me to ask the abbot. I have asked the abbot.
We are not going to Deas. Nobody has asked us, and the beds do not walk.
I am to stay for the lamp, they say. One lamp. I learned to count as far as three for this house, and now look.
Three heaps of the year's salt stand under rush thatch above the tide line: one for the abbot, one for the islanders' lord, and one that has always been argued over.
A woman you carried over the lagoon on the feast day puts a loaf in your hand and says nothing.
Tell them all of it, and help carry the third heap to the lagoon side
Tell them, then go up to the abbot with Martinus and ask what he will leave
Say only that the abbot has been to the king, and let them work it out

You tell it: the king's leave, the morning flood, Deas. Nobody shouts. By the next ebb the third heap is under rushes in the dunes on the lagoon side, and four sacks of it are in your hold. The abbot will count two heaps and know why.

Hilbod hears Martinus out standing up. Then he sends for a leaf and has it written: a priest and two brothers to stay, the wall's men paid to Michaelmas, a third of the salt to the rakers. He hands it to you, not to Martinus, and says: you will carry him, then, and they will let you.

Hilbod says the saint is not the island's to keep or to bargain over, and that he had thought better of a shipman than to bring him a raker with a list. Martinus says nothing all the way down the path. The third heap is gone by morning.
Martinus looks at you for a while. He says an abbot does not go to a king to ask leave to stay where he is, and goes back to his rake.
Lead in a shed
Riwal, a Breton master who brings grain to the bay and takes away only salt, has looked through the cracks of the monks' shed at Furca.
There is a church roof lying on the ground at Furca, rolled up like cloth. The keeper drinks. He will sell some of it and not see the rest go.
Not here. Round on the Seine there are abbeys with the rain coming in. Your hull, my buyer, a third to you. Lead has no face.
The monks took it off the saint's house themselves. I only mean to take it a little further.
His ship has a yard, a sail and two anchors, and sits low with rye. His steersman and his bow man watch you from the rail and do not smile.
Take the third share
No. Leave that shed alone
Go to the abbot's man with it

It is done on a dark ebb at Furca, part bought from the keeper and part not. The sheets go under the salt in both hulls. Riwal's bow man crosses himself as each one comes aboard, and Riwal tells him to stop counting.
Riwal shrugs and says there are other hulls. He does not seem to hold it against you. He does not seem to give up the shed either.

The abbey's man at the quay hears you out and goes white. A new keeper is at Furca within the week. Hilbod sends thirty pennies, and an order: when the roof at Deas is ready for it he will want more lead than he has, and he would sooner buy it from you.
The seventh day of June
The founder of the house leaves his island in his marble coffin, by ship for Furca and then by road to Deas.
The tenth morning after Pentecost. The coffin comes down the path from the west gate on its frame, eight brothers under it and the rest singing. The flood is making in the channel.
One tide. Afloat at the top of the flood, out by the channel before it dries, Furca on the north-west wind. If she touches, he sits on a sand bar for the whole bay to look at.
What is your ship called, and your father? I am writing it all down. It is the third hour, unless I am mistaken, and I would be glad if you told me so.
There is a pit in the floor of the basilica and a bare step where the coffin stood. One lamp burns where there were three. He went on the seventh day of June, on a flat sea, and you were not here.
He blessed this salt, they say. Stand where you like, shipman. I know where I am standing.
A priest and two brothers are staying, and the wall's men are paid to Michaelmas. It is written on a leaf, and Martinus has had it read to him twice.
Some lead came back to Furca in sheets. We have cast it in lumps. I do not ask where it had been.
Take the coffin aboard at the top of the flood
Let the abbey's own boat take him. Carry the house's goods and the last of the lead
Stand on the sand with the rakers

She floats with a hand's breadth to spare and goes down the channel like a led horse. The wind is north-west and the sea lies flat. At Furca the brothers lift him out singing, and Hilbod stands a moment with his hand on your stem before he follows.

She touches at the bend and the ebb leaves her. Saint Philibert sits a whole tide on a sand bar in your hold, with the brothers standing round him in the wet, singing the hours. On the night flood she lifts. He is at Furca by first light. Nobody in your crew speaks until then.
Chests, vestments, the cellarer's tallies, a bell and a load of lead in lumps: you set them down dry at Furca and are paid 180 pennies. The monks thank you as they would a carter.
You stand at the tide line among the rakes. Nobody on the sand sings. When the sail is small Martinus says, well, and goes up to the basilica to see how many lamps they have left him.
No wind off Batz
With the monks' lead under the salt, the wind dies off the island of Batz and does not come back. Riwal's ship lies a bowshot off, as still as yours.
A rider. On the water, there, coming up from the south. A white horse, and three spears in his hand. Do not tell me it was a gull.
My bow man has seen it too. He wants to go back. I have told him lead is heavy and visions are light.
At dusk a fishing boat rows out from Batz. They have a lame man ashore who woke this morning walking, and he says a monk in his dream told him why the two ships have no wind.
Put about and take it back to Furca
Out oars. Saints do not ride on water
Vow the saint a tenth of the price and a lamp's oil, and wait

The wind comes before the oars are out, from the north, fair for Furca and for nowhere else. Riwal calls you several things across the water and then, a while later, follows. The sheets go back into the shed by night. No one is ever asked about it.
A day and a night at the oars, and at the second dawn a little air from the west. Nobody saw the rider again. Nobody looked south.

Three days at the oars on a sea like oil, the water cask down to the lees, and the bow man seeing spears in every gull. The wind that comes at last is foul. You make the Seine all the same, with a crew that has stopped looking at you.
You say it aloud, on the lead, with the crew as witnesses: a tenth and a lamp's oil. The air comes within the hour. Riwal says it would have come anyway. He does not say it very loud.
A guest of Saint Philibert
The saint reached Deas on men's shoulders in four days. At Namnetis the abbot settles his accounts before the summer is out.
They say the sick were healed all along the road, at Ampan, at Varenne, at Paulx. And that for this one year women may come in to the tomb at Deas, from feast to feast.
You brought her in on the tide I named. I have thanked God. Now I thank you, by name.
She touched, and he sat a tide on the sand with the brothers singing round him to keep the gulls off. He is at Deas all the same. I count the end.
The goods came dry and the lead came whole. That is a carter's praise, and I mean it as praise.
I shall write that the sea lay flat for him. I shall not name the ship; the book is about the saint. But the house will know.
Is anyone left on the island to say Mass?
You can tell the bishop yes: a priest, two brothers and a paid wall. He shuts his eyes for a moment.
They are calling it faint heart in the city. Let them. The bones are where a count can reach them.
Ask for a guest's place wherever the saint lies
Ask for room in the abbey's six boats on the Loire, toll-free
Ask for the guest's place, and for the island's share to be kept as it was written
Take the carter's fee, and the coffin's frame and rollers

Three pounds of pennies from the abbot's chest, and a thing that is not in any chest: wherever the body rests, a merchant of your line has a bed, a hearing and a place at the guest table. Hilbod says it before the bishop so that it will be remembered.

Two and a half pounds of pennies, and the abbey's man at the quay is told that your goods ride in the saint's boats when there is room. The king's toll does not touch what the saint carries. The toll man will learn your face and dislike it.

Hilbod is silent, then laughs once. Five pounds of pennies, the guest's place for your line, and the leaf about the island's third copied fair with the bishop's mark under it. Martinus is to keep your tally on the island. The abbot says he has been out-measured, and does not seem sorry.

The fee is counted out and is fair. The oak frame and the rollers that took a marble coffin down a beach are no use to the monks now; they are fitted to your ship, and will bring her up any sand you choose.
One lamp
The saint's feast comes round with no saint. The islanders keep it anyway, on the sand, and count what the monks left.
One lamp where there were three. I trim it. Nobody told me to.
What did they say about me at Furca? No. Do not tell me.
The third heap went to a Breton for rye and silver while the abbot was counting stalls at Deas. Your share is in the dune under rushes, like everything of ours.
The abbot took two heaps and left the one nobody could ever agree on. We have agreed. Part of it is yours, for standing where you stood.
The fort stands with eleven men on it. Bread is still baked for the windbound, by a woman now, which is new.
Word from Deas is that the abbot knows who talked. He has not cursed you. He has stopped asking after you.
Leave your tally and your salt with Martinus
Ask for a berth on the lagoon side and a store dug in the dune
Take part of your share in salt, and a raker's welcome

Your share comes to 640 pennies, counted on a raking board. Martinus splits a tally stick and keeps half: from now on your salt waits on this island under his eye, and is sold or held as you tell him.

Six hundred pennies, and a place the monks never knew about: a berth behind the dunes on the lagoon side where a boat cannot be seen from the bay, with a store dug into the sand beside it. The rakers dig it in a day and roof it with a dead man's boat.

Ten sacks of the white salt off the top of the heap, the rest in pennies, and your half of a tally stick. The woman with the rake calls you her son. You have heard what she calls merchants who cheat her, and take it as meant.
Three lamps
The saint's feast, and the marble coffin lies where it has lain since the founder died. The count's men are on the wall, and a flat ferry lies at Furca.
The vigil is kept through the night, as it was the year of the nine ships. At the ninth hour every man on the wall looks at the east head. Nothing comes round it but terns.
I had the king's leave to go and I have not used it. If I am wrong, shipman, we are both in the young brother's book, and not in the chapter either of us would choose.
Twenty men on the wall, changed at each new moon, over your road. They complain of the salt wind. Good. A man who complains is awake.
The big tide took nine withies. I have cut nine more. That is every spring from now on, and somebody must do it or pay for it.
I had begun a book about a journey. Now it is a book about a tomb, which is shorter, unless I am mistaken, and may be better.
Take the locked store inside the wall
Take the ferry at Furca for your house, with its fare
Ask only that your name be said at the tomb

A stone-footed store against the inside of the bank, with a lock and one key, and 900 pennies from the count and the abbot between them. You know the channel now as the islanders know it. The withies are yours to keep standing, every spring.

The flat boat at Furca is your house's, with a fare from every man and beast that crosses and three pounds of pennies for the year past. The count's men cross free; that was the bargain. The withies are yours to keep standing, every spring.

Hilbod looks at you a long time. Your name is said at the tomb that night, after the founder's and before the king's, and will be said each year. He sends two and a half pounds of pennies to the boat anyway, and a guest's place for your line. The withies are yours to keep standing, every spring.
Whose roof it was
At Rotomagus the cellarer of Jumieges is buying lead for a leaking aisle. Jumieges is the first house Saint Philibert founded, two tides down the river.
Good sheet. Old work, with nail holes along one edge. This has been on a roof. Whose?
Our founder went from here to an island in the south and built again. We keep his day at the end of harvest. You will have heard of him, coming from that way.
English lead. Everybody knows the English have hills of it. Tell him, friend.
Two of your men have not spoken to you since the calm. One of them crosses himself each time the cellarer says the founder's name.
You vowed a tenth and a lamp's oil off Batz, and the wind came within the hour.
Say it came from the English, and sell
Sell, and set a tenth and a lamp's oil aside for the saint
Tell the cellarer whose roof it was

The cellarer pays by weight and asks nothing more. Your third is 1,100 pennies. Riwal drinks with you on it and swears partnership, his hull beside yours from now on. Saint Philibert's lead goes up on Saint Philibert's first roof, and only you, a Breton and the saint know.

You sell, and count a tenth into a separate bag before Riwal can speak, with the price of a jar of oil on top: it goes south by the next ship for the lamps. He calls it a waste and swears partnership all the same. Your men talk to you again.

The cellarer sits down on the lead. Then he pays you a finder's price, 650 pennies, has a letter written to Abbot Hilbod, and keeps the sheets until an answer comes. He says a house that owes you its founder's roof can keep your goods under its own at the quay. Riwal has already cast off.
The first book
Abbot Hilduin of Saint-Denis has been sent a book of the wonders of Saint Philibert by a young monk of the west, to be corrected. He has heard that you were there.
A young monk of the west has sent me a book of his saint's wonders to correct. He writes well and counts boldly. You were there, shipman. Sit.
They tell of four hundred and eighty-four heathen dead on a feast day, and one of ours. I am an abbot; I should like it to be true. I am also asked to correct.
There is a chapter here about shipmen and a church's lead, and a rider on the sea with three spears. You have gone a strange colour.
And this I do not follow at all. He had the king's leave to move the body, and he stayed. Whose counsel was that?
Eight monks are singing in the new chapel and can be heard through the wall. A clerk holds the quire open with two fingers and waits.
Tell it as you saw it
Tell it as the monks tell it
Say a shipman counts tides, not miracles

You tell him: the mound above the tide line, the channel, the hour of the flood. He has the clerk read you each sentence in Latin and then in plain speech, and by the end you are following some of the Latin. He changes nothing in the book. He says the boy may count as he likes, so long as somebody once counted properly. Sixty pennies, and an order for skins.

You give him the saint in white and the golden sword. Hilduin listens with his eyes shut and has a hundred pennies sent to your boat. At the door he says he had hoped to meet a witness, and has met a second copy.
Hilduin says that is the most honest answer he has had in a year of asking, and lets you go back to your casks.
On the feast of Saint Philibert nine ships of the Northmen came to the island of Herio. The count of Herbauge and the abbey's men fought them from the ninth hour until evening and beat them off.
This year the monks of Herio took the body of Saint Philibert out of his island for fear of the Northmen, and carried it to Deas on the mainland. The sick were healed along the road.
This year the abbot of Herio had the king's leave to carry Saint Philibert off his island, and did not. The count keeps men on the abbey's wall, and there is a ferry over the channel.

A low sandy island under a wide grey-bright sky, mid-morning: in front, lay workers driving squared oak stakes into a fresh turf bank; a square weathered abbot in a muddy black habit measures the gap with a rod; an old sunburnt monk white to the knee with salt leans on a long rake, grinning; behind, a stone basilica with half its roof stripped to bare rafters.

Under the towered Roman wall of Burdigala by the brown Garonne, hot afternoon light: a stout oil seller in a belted linen tunic stands among tall clay jars bedded in straw, one hand flat on a jar scratched with a cross, the other holding a tally stick; a small ship lies idle at the bank behind him, her yard lowered.

The west gate of a turf-and-timber rampart on Herio, late afternoon, flat calm sea: nine low ships beached on wet sand, raiders running up the shore; Frankish horsemen wheeling on the hard ground; at the gate a line of the abbey's armed men with round shields; small in the dunes to one side, a boat crowded with children pushing off across a lagoon.

A bishop's hall at Namnetis, autumn daylight from a high window: a slight grey bishop in a white alb leaning forward to listen; a square abbot standing with a sealed parchment in one hand and a measuring rod in the other; a Frankish count in a riding cloak with his arms folded; a merchant in sea clothes before them, a rough map of a channel drawn in spilt wine on the table.

A tidal channel between an island and the mainland at half tide, bright windy spring morning: a line of tall withies marching across brown water, doubled at the bend; a flat ferry with four nervous horses and mailed riders poled by islanders; a lean young salter at the bow with a sounding pole ringed in red wool; on the far sand a count on horseback, watching.

The salt heaps of Herio at low sun, evening: three long heaps under rush thatch above the tide line; a ring of islanders with wooden rakes, men and women, bare-legged, facing a merchant; a lean young salter in front with his arms crossed; an old monk sitting apart on an upturned basket, counting on three fingers.

The quay at Namnetis under the Roman wall, dusk, drizzle: a dark wiry Breton master in a hooded cloak talking low with one hand cupped as if weighing something; behind him a beamy sea ship with yard, sail and two anchors, low in the water with grain, a steersman and a bow man staring from the rail.

The beach of Conca on Herio, clear early morning, the flood making: a white marble coffin on a wooden frame carried down the sand on the shoulders of eight monks toward a small ship held in the shallows; an abbot with a measuring rod walking ahead; a young short-sighted monk writing on a wax tablet; islanders standing silent along the tide line with their rakes.

Two ships lying still on a sea like oil off a low rocky island, late afternoon haze, sails hanging slack: on the nearer ship a bow man points south with his whole arm, the crew turned to look; far off on the shining water, small and not quite certain, a rider on a white horse with three spears.

The bishop's house at Namnetis, a summer evening, door open on the Loire: a square abbot counting pennies from a small chest onto a table; a slight bishop beside him with a plain silver cross; a young monk with a wax tablet round his neck writing; in the doorway, leaning against the post, an oak carrying frame and rollers.

Inside the basilica of Herio, dim, evening: an open pit in the floor and a bare stone step; one small lamp burning on an iron stand where three hooks hang; a lean young salter trimming the wick with a knife, a rake propped against the wall; through the open door, islanders eating together on the sand.

The basilica of Herio at night on the saint's feast: a white marble coffin under three burning lamps, monks singing in full stalls; through a window, torchlight on a turf rampart with spearmen looking seaward; an abbot and a Frankish count standing side by side at the back, not singing, watching the door.

The river gate quay at Rotomagus, grey morning, the Seine at high tide: rolled sheets of old lead with nail holes laid out on the stones; a heavy monk cellarer crouched over them with a steelyard, looking up sharply; a Breton master smiling too widely beside him; a merchant between the two, looking at the lead.

A room in the abbey of Saint-Denis, clear north light: a tall elderly abbot seated with an unbound quire of parchment on his knee, one finger on a line; a clerk holding the leaves open; a merchant on a stool opposite, cap in hand; through an inner door, monks singing in a small chapel lit by candles.

A country road through marsh and vines on the mainland, summer noon: a marble coffin on a frame carried on men's shoulders at the head of a long line of monks and country people, the sick laid at the roadside reaching to touch its cloth; far behind, small on the sea, a low island.

The lagoon side of Herio at dawn, mist on the water: a small trading boat lying hidden behind dunes; beside her a store dug into the sand and roofed with an upturned old boat; a salter handing half a split tally stick to a merchant; salt heaps under rushes.

Herio from the sea on a flat calm summer day: a turf-and-timber fort with spearmen along its rampart round a stone church with a whole lead roof; a line of withies crossing the channel to the mainland and a flat ferry half way over with horses; no sail anywhere on the horizon.

The abbey of Jumieges on a bend of the Seine in rain: workmen on a church roof nailing down sheets of old lead; below, a Breton ship and a small trader moored side by side, two masters shaking hands over a bag of silver; at the rail, a crewman crossing himself.
